Anvil
AN-vil
n. (an iron block on which metal is hammered into shape)
Old English anfilte, that on which a thing is beaten out, from an- (on) and a root meaning to strike. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Isaiah's mockery of the idol factory, where the anvil is the bed on which men beat out the god they will afterward pray to.

Biblical Definition

The anvil appears one time in Scripture, and it appears inside a satire. Isaiah is describing the assembly line of idolatry: carpenter encouraging goldsmith, one man smoothing with the hammer and cheering on the man who smote the anvil, the whole shop congratulating itself that the soldering is ready, and then fastening the finished deity down with nails so that it should not be moved. Every tool in the shop is a real tool doing real work. The iron is honest iron and the workmanship is honest workmanship; what is dishonest is the object. A god that must be nailed in place lest it topple is not a god, and Isaiah lets the tools tell us so without a word of direct argument. The anvil therefore belongs to the dictionary's doctrine of labour as much as to its doctrine of idols. God gave men hammers and anvils and the skill to use them, and that skill is a common grace. The question the anvil asks is not whether a man may beat iron, but what he intends to set up when the beating is done. The same forge that makes a plough makes a graven image, and the difference lies not in the iron but in the heart of the man at the bellows.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): an iron block with a smooth face, on which smiths hammer and shape their work; figuratively, whatever is beaten or wrought upon.

expand to see more

ANVIL, n. An iron block with a smooth face, on which smiths hammer and shape their work.

ANVIL, n. Figuratively, any thing on which blows are laid; to be on the anvil, to be in a state of formation or preparation.

SMITH, n. One who works in metals; one who forges with the hammer.

FORGE, n. A furnace in which iron is heated and wrought; the place where anything is fashioned.

IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.

Key Scripture

Isa 41:7 — "So the carpenter encouraged the goldsmith, and he that smootheth with the hammer him that smote the anvil, saying, It is ready for the sodering: and he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved."

Isa 44:12 — "The smith with the tongs both worketh in the coals, and fashioneth it with hammers, and worketh it with the strength of his arms: yea, he is hungry, and his strength faileth: he drinketh no water, and is faint."

Isa 40:19 — "The workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold, and casteth silver chains."

Psa 115:4 — "Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands."

Modern Corruption

Craftsmanship is spoken of as if skill itself sanctified what skill produces, so that excellence in the making is treated as a warrant for the thing made; Isaiah's idol shop is excellent work in the service of a lie.

expand to see more

The modern celebration of craft as a nearly sacramental good runs straight into Isaiah 41:7. The shop in that verse is a good shop. The men encourage one another, the hammer work is fine, the soldering holds, the joints are true. Isaiah does not fault a single operation. He faults the product, and by faulting the product while praising nothing else he exposes the whole trade of self-made religion. Skill is a gift of God and remains a gift when it is bent; a forger's hand is often steadier than an honest man's. The dictionary therefore refuses the flattery that treats excellence as its own justification. Ask first what is on the anvil.

The second corruption is subtler and older: the assumption that a god men can secure is a god worth having. The workman fastens the image with nails that it should not be moved, and the whole logic of manageable religion is in that clause. The living God is the one who cannot be steadied, arranged, relocated, or improved, and men have always preferred the other kind. A faith adjusted until it sits quietly where it was set, offends no one, and never speaks back is an idol with better manners, and the nails are still in it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pa'am (H6471), a beat or stroke, rendered anvil in Isaiah 41:7; halam (H1986), to smite or hammer; charash (H2796), a craftsman.

expand to see more

Hebrew pa'am (H6471) — a stroke, a beat, a time; the struck block, and so the anvil of Isaiah 41:7.

Hebrew halam (H1986) — to smite, to hammer, to beat down; the verb of the man at the anvil.

Hebrew charash (H2796) — an engraver or artificer in wood, stone, or metal; the carpenter and the smith alike.

Hebrew tsaraph (H6884) — to refine or smelt; the goldsmith of the same verse, and the refiner of Malachi 3:3.

Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a graven image; what came off the anvil in Isaiah's shop.

Usage

"“him that smote the anvil” — the one occurrence, inside a satire on idol-making."

"“he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved” — a god that must be steadied."

"The anvil as an emblem of honest labour that can be bent to dishonest ends."
